explanation: Fires on words for connecting or joining things, chiefly 'coupled'/'coupling' (mechanical couplings, physical or chemical coupling, 'coupled with' in instrument names such as inductively coupled plasma) and 'joint'/'Joint' (body or mechanical joints, Joint Committee, joint venture). It fires moderately on nearby ideas such as articulated, clutch, ligand, couples and league, and barely at all elsewhere.

No single concept. It fires mostly on punctuation and syntax tokens inside code (')', '::', '").', ',', ':', quotes, '=' in formulas, '().'), and also on scattered mid-word or function-word tokens in prose and in other languages (won['t], Ball[iol], Japanese particles, 'than'). It is hard to predict beyond 'a code-syntax token somewhere in the middle of an expression'.

Fires on genetics, breeding and evolution vocabulary: crossed/cross, mating, offspring, diploids, mutations, recombination, germ line, reproduction, selection, progenitor, clonal, evolution, genetic diversity and parents/progeny. It is strongest for crossing and breeding in a genetics context, and only weak on unrelated tokens.

Fires on filler and framing words near the start of formal or expository sentences, most of all 'example' in 'for example' / 'such as, for example' and 'e.g.', along with 'in general', 'relates generally', 'such as' and boilerplate patent or intro phrasing. It fires more weakly on other function words early in casual sentences ('In my', 'we've', 'over on').

Fires on the return type 'void' in method declarations in Java, C#, C++ or Objective-C, strongest in 'public static void main' and in 'private/public void Name(' and '- (void)'. Outside that it is near zero, apart from weak, scattered activations.

Fires on the token that opens the top-level type declaration of a source file: 'public' right after the import/package/comment header in Java (public class/interface), and in C# the '{' or 'public' right after a namespace line. Activations outside code are weak and scattered.

Fires on the first '0' of the thousands group right after the comma in comma-formatted numbers (e.g. 231,[0]00 or $120,[0]00), whatever the topic. It fires moderately on the token right after a comma in other places (', making', ', with', a digit after a comma).

Fires on the first sub-word piece of a word that the tokenizer has split into pieces, especially in non-English text (French, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Russian) and in technical or medical terms, e.g. '[S]ouligné', '[К]орзина', '[m]airie', '[p]ustules', 'Dros[oph]ila'. What matters is that the token begins a multi-token word, not what it means.

Fires on 'for' (and on the period or newline ending the line) in counsel-appearance lines of legal opinions, e.g. 'John Smith, Asst. Atty. Gen., [for] appellant.' It fires on a few unrelated tokens too ('Share [this] post', 'Hind [III]'), but its main job is the attorney-for-party line.

Fires on a capital or lowercase 'N' (and some other short starts such as 'El', 'sn', 'Fl') when it is the first piece of a split proper noun or acronym, most of all in sports and organization names (NCHC, NBA, NBL, NMSU, Nittany, Nascar, Ntilikina, Niterói). The token needs to be the first piece of a word the tokenizer has split, and the N-initial case is strongest.

Fires on sub-word pieces in the middle of rare or foreign words and names that are split into several tokens (dend[rim]ers, te[hs]ils, Ad[ir]ondack, alk[oh]olikere, Quercus [rob]ur, d[iph]theria), with some whole words in place names or titles. It is a general 'inside an unusual multi-token word' unit with no semantic focus.

A mixture. It fires strongly on the token 'bol'/'Bol' (bolus, Bolin, Bolts, boliviensis, bollocks), on punctuation in code (commas between JS object arguments, ':' in Ruby hashes, '<link', '"></script>', ' =', a quoted string argument) and on '/c' or '/D' after a slash, plus scattered tokens from medical and biology text.

Fires mainly on terms inside polynomial expressions in math word problems: the exponent '2' in 'x**2' and terms such as '*i', '*a', ' l' in 'Let f(x) = ...'. It also fires on math and statistics jargon (coefficient of determination, inverse, first order, factor analyses), and weakly on unrelated tokens.

No clear shared feature. It fires on Chinese pronoun and modal phrases (你可以, 我, 没有), on 'you can' and 'You May Also', on regex or function-call openers in code ('(/', '("', '({', '.sub', '($'), and on assorted nouns in technical prose (power spectrum, lattice, energy, intellectual property).
